Then the Lord of Might, glorified is He, says:

﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do.﴾ (24:30)

The surah of al-Nur, from its beginning, has spoken of the matter of fornication (zina), slander (qadhf) and chastity (ihsan). It has warned against following the steps of Satan (khutuwat al-shaytan), which lead to this crime, and it has spoken of equality (takafu') in marriage: that the adulterer marries only an adulteress or a polytheist, and that the adulteress is married only to an adulterer or a polytheist, that the foul (al-khabithun) are for the foul (al-khabithat), and the good (al-tayyibun) are for the good (al-tayyibat).

This is a comprehensive method (manhaj mutakamil) that guarantees the safety of society and the vicegerency of Allah on His earth. Allah, exalted is He, desires a society in which noble values shine, a society free of the means of disturbance (al-'uknna), opposition, rancour and hatred. If we applied the method of Allah which He has chosen for us, everyone would find rest under its shade.

The matter of lowering the gaze, which our Lord, Mighty and Majestic, commands us in this verse, is the safety valve that protects us from slipping into these abominable crimes and blocks the path leading to them. Therefore, Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze..﴾ (24:30).

We have said that a human being has several means of perception, and each organ of perception has its own domain: the ear hears sound, the nose smells odour, the tongue is for speech and for tasting food, and the eye is for seeing what is seen. But the most seductive thing that befalls a person in respect of sexuality is the sense of sight. Therefore the Wise Lawgiver (al-Shari' al-Hakim) placed the necessary immunity at both ends of vision: in the seeing eye and in the thing seen. He commanded the believing men to lower their gaze, and commanded the believing women not to display their adornment (zina). Thus He made immunity present at both ends.

If you reflect on the matter of lowering the gaze, you find that, in terms of rational division, it revolves around four situations:
The first: he lowers his gaze and she does not display her adornment. The line of temptation is cut off from both the sender and the receiver.
The second: he lowers his gaze and she displays her adornment.
The third: he looks and she does not display her adornment.
There is no danger to society or temptation in these three situations; whenever one side is present, the other is absent. The danger lies only in the fourth division: that he looks and does not lower his gaze, and she adorns herself and displays her adornment. Only in this case is there danger.

So, the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, forbade one situation out of four, because the prohibited things are always fewer, and this is from the mercy of Allah towards us, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden to you..﴾ (6:151). The prohibited things are the limited and counted ones, whereas the permitted things are beyond count and enumeration. The default regarding things is that they are permissible, and when Allah, glorified is He, wishes to prohibit something, He states it explicitly. So look at this good dealing from your Lord, Mighty and Majestic.

Just as the man is commanded to lower his gaze, so too the woman is commanded to lower her gaze, because a glance may also be directed at a handsome man, and... If the woman's share is a man at whom the eye is drawn, she may look at someone else; just as is said of men, so is said of women.

This precaution and these limits which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has set and obligated us to observe, are only to prevent this abominable crime with which this surah began, because the gaze is the first means of fornication, and it is the messenger for what follows. Do you not see that Shawqi, may Allah have mercy on him, when he spoke of the stages of courtship, said:
"A glance, then a smile, then a greeting, * then speech, then an appointment, then a meeting."

Thus the command to lower the gaze is to close the outlets of the corruption of honour and to prevent the causes of the contamination of lineage, so that the vicegerent of Allah on earth may come forth pure, in a pure, clean and noble society in which no one exalts himself over another on the ground that he has lineage and honour while the other has no lineage.

This is so that every person may be assured that those who come after him in succession, whether sons or grandsons, came through a lawful and noble path. Each person will strive to raise his children with tenderness, affection and mercy, because he is confident that they are his own child, not one foisted upon him. Indeed, it is most likely that those who neglect their children and do not attend to their welfare doubt their lineage to them.

Society will not reach this purity unless it is given sufficient protection, lest the instincts of sex run wild in it, so that every gaze transgresses onto what is not lawful for it, because the gaze is a messenger to the hearts, and the hearts are a messenger to sexuality. Chastity of the private parts is not achieved except through chastity of the gaze.

We note in His saying: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze..﴾ (24:30) the precision of the Messenger's conveying from his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and his trustworthiness in transmitting the wording as it was revealed to him. In this verse it would have sufficed for the Messenger of Allah to say: "Lower your gazes," but he adhered to the exact text that was revealed to him, because the Qur'an was not revealed for rulings alone; rather, the Qur'an is the speech of Allah revealed to His Messenger, which is worshipped by its recitation, so the Messenger must convey it exactly as it came to him from his Lord.

Therefore, in conveying from Allah He said "Say" (qul), and the verb "yaghuddu" (they should lower) indicates the significance of "qul." The verb yaghudu is a present-tense verb not preceded by a jussive particle, yet the nun was dropped from it, because He made "qul" have a significant place in the style.

The meaning is: if you say to them "lower your gazes," they will lower them. So the verb is, therefore, in the jussive mood as the answer to the imperative "qul."

Thus ﴿Say..﴾ (24:30) indicates the trustworthiness of the Messenger in conveying, and that the Qur'an was not revealed for rulings only, but is also the inimitable speech of Allah; therefore we preserve it and every word in it. It is as if the Messenger of Allah (ṣ) says: "I have not brought you anything from myself; my task is to convey to you what Allah has said to me."

As for His saying: ﴿To the believing men..﴾ (24:30): since they are believers in a Wise God, and have entered the enclosure of faith by their own choice, no one compelled them to it, they must abide by what their Lord has commanded them and implement it as soon as they hear it.

Al-ghadd (lowering) means diminishing: it is said, "So-and-so lowers the status of so-and-so," meaning he diminishes it. How, then, can there be diminution in sight? Does one look with one eye? They say: sight has a function, and through it the seen things are manifested, and the eye's domain is free, seeing everything in front of it, whether it is lawful for it or forbidden to it.

So the diminishing of sight means restricting it to what is permitted and restraining it from what is forbidden. The diminishing is a diminution in the objects seen and in the field of vision: it is not given absolute freedom to look at everything, but is halted at the commands of Allah regarding what it sees and what it does not see.

As for "min" in ﴿from their gazes..﴾ (24:30): some hold that it is partitive (lil-tab'id), as you say "I ate some (min) of this food," meaning a part of it. So the meaning is: "they should lower some of their sight," because part of it is lawful (I do not lower my gaze from it) and part of it is forbidden (I do not look at it).

Or: the "min" here is to emphasise generality at its least degree. We have previously discussed "min" in this sense, and whenever we go deeper into the tafsir, things we have mentioned earlier must come before us, and we refer the reader back to them.

We have said: there is a difference between your saying "ma 'indi mal" (I have no wealth) and your saying "ma 'indi min mal" (I have no wealth at all). "Ma 'indi mal" may imply that you have a little wealth that is not considered significant, but "ma 'indi min mal" is a negation of the category of wealth, however little it may be: so "min" here means the beginning of what is called wealth.

So the meaning here: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gazes..﴾ (24:30) means: the beginning of what is called sight, even a fleeting glance, let alone contemplation and prolonged looking.

We have said that the Shari'ah does not intervene in heart-felt impulses and passing thoughts, but intervenes in the impulsive acts which lead to an action. We have said: if you pass by an orchard and see a beautiful rose in it, and you admire it, are delighted by it, and the features of your soul brighten towards it, all of this is permissible for you, with no blame on you. But if the matter goes beyond that, and you extend your hand to pluck it, here the Shari'ah intervenes and tells you: "Stop, this is not your right, for it is not yours."

This is a general rule in all actions, from which only the gaze is excluded. It is as if our Lord, Mighty and Majestic, is asking our indulgence regarding it: this matter is for our sake, for our benefit, for our comfort; rather, say it is mercy towards us and compassion for us from the consequences of the gaze and what it leaves in the soul of torments and agitations.

So, regarding a man's gaze at a woman, we do not say to him: "Look as you like and love as you wish." If he then inclines towards an embrace or a kiss, we say to you: "It is forbidden." Why? Because the matter here is entirely different: a man's relationship with a woman has stages, none of which is ever separated from the others.

When you look at a woman, this is perception (idrak). If she pleases you and the features of your face brighten towards her, this is feeling (wijdan), which must leave in your make-up a chemical reaction that does not subside, unless you yearn (nuzu'). If you obey your self in the yearning, you have transgressed; and if these feelings are suppressed within you, they afflict you with psychological complexes and call you to seek another means of yearning. Therefore your Lord has shown you mercy from the very beginning and called you to prevent perception by lowering the gaze.

Therefore, after commanding us to lower the gaze, He said: ﴿and guard their private parts..﴾ (24:30), because you cannot separate yearning from feeling, nor feeling from perception, although that may be possible in other matters. When we prevent you from plucking the rose that pleased you, this prohibition leaves no trace or passion in your soul, unlike what happens if you are prevented from a woman who pleased you and whose feeling has stirred you towards her.

Guarding the private parts means restricting them to what Allah has made lawful and prescribed, so they are not granted to anyone not lawfully permitted to them, whether from the man or the woman. Or: guard them and protect them from being seen, because seeing them stirs towards evil and temptation.

﴿That is purer for them..﴾ (24:30): meaning more pure, safer, and more conducive to the ease of the soul, because either he yearns and so commits a prohibited act and intrudes upon people's honour, or he does not yearn and so troubles his soul and pains it by enduring what it cannot bear.

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do.﴾ (24:30): He, glorified is He, is the Creator of this human soul and the One who established the matter of desire and the sexual instinct, the strongest of instincts, by which He links man and woman, and by which He accomplishes reproduction and the continuation of vicegerency on earth. Had this relationship not been tied to urgent desire, many would have renounced marriage and childbearing and the consequences that follow from them.

Do you not see the woman and what she suffers of pains and hardships during pregnancy, and that she sees death at childbirth, to the point that she swears she will never return to it? But after she sees her newborn and forgets her pains, the longing to bear again quickly returns to her. It is the instinct that Allah planted in the human soul for its continued survival.

Some have a philosophical view of the instincts: especially the instinct of sex, which Allah, exalted is He, made the strongest of instincts and linked to a pleasure more potent than the pleasure of food, drink, smell and hearing, and so on. It is a pleasure that encompasses all of the human's faculties and powers, and this is nothing but a desire for the preservation of the species and the continuation of vicegerency on earth.

Then the Truthful, glorified is He, says to His Messenger:

﴿And say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze, guard their private parts, and not display their adornment except what appears thereof; and let them draw their head-coverings over their chests, and not display their adornment except to their husbands, or their fathers, or their husbands' fathers, or their sons, or their husbands' sons, or their brothers, or their brothers' sons, or their sisters' sons, or their women, or those whom their right hands possess, or male attendants who have no physical desire, or children who are not yet aware of the private aspects of women. And let them not stamp their feet so as to reveal what they hide of their adornment. And turn to Allah in repentance, all of you, O believers, so that you may succeed.﴾ (24:31)

Here He mentions the counterpart: He commands the women with what He commanded the men, then adds here the matter of adornment. Adornment (zina) is that which exceeds the natural limit of beauty. Hence they say of a woman who is beautiful by nature and does not need to adorn herself: ghaniyah (a woman who is self-sufficient), meaning she has been made independent of adornment by her beauty, so she needs no kohl for her eyes, no rouge for her cheeks, and does not need to cover her wrist with bracelets or her chest with a necklace, and so on.

If a woman is below this level, she needs some adornment. But it is strange that they exaggerate in this adornment until it becomes like a neon sign on a leaning wooden kiosk. You see older women applying these colours and these cosmetics, so they appear in a form that is not becoming, because it is artificial beauty and forced adornment, which they call tatriyah (rejuvenation). About this al-Mutanabbi said, describing the beauty of the Bedouin woman and the beauty of the urban woman:

"The beauty of civilisation is acquired through rejuvenation, while in the desert there is a beauty that is not acquired."

And from Allah's mercy towards women is that after ﴿and not display their adornment…﴾ He said ﴿except what appears thereof…﴾: meaning the necessary things. A woman needs to walk in the street, so her eyes may be seen, and perhaps there is kohl in them, for example, and her hand may be seen, and on it a ring or henna; there is no harm in displaying such necessary adornment.

But something like the earring, for example, must not be displayed, because the headcover conceals it; nor the décolletage, the necklace, the bracelet, the armlet, or the anklet; these are adornments that should not be displayed. Thus the Lawgiver permitted natural adornment on condition that it is within limits, and that it be restricted to the one for whom it was made.

We observe in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and not display their adornment except what appears thereof…﴾ that the intent is to cover the adornment, so the body part beneath it is covered all the more; the adornment covers the body part, and Allah has commanded the concealing of adornment, so the body part is covered all the more.

As for His saying: ﴿and let them draw their head-coverings over their chests…﴾:

Khumur is the plural of khimar, which is the head covering that is let down to conceal the neck and chest. Juyub is the plural of jayb, which is the upper opening of a garment, and which they call the qubbah (neckline). The intent is that the khimar should cover the opening of the garment and the area of the chest, so that nothing of it appears.

It is strange that women have abandoned this duty; and among the contradictions is that they wear necklaces and hang from them the noble Qur'an, a strange contradiction that indicates lack of awareness and lack of understanding of the law of Allah that revealed this Qur'an.

Consider the precision of the Qur'anic expression in His saying: ﴿and let them draw…﴾ (wa-liyadribna). Ḍarb is a forceful striking; so the intent is not that a woman places the veil on her head and leaves it thus to the wind, but rather she must secure it on her head and chest and tie it firmly.

Therefore, when this verse was revealed, Sayyidah 'Aishah said: "May Allah have mercy on the women of the Muhajirat. When this verse was revealed, they did not have khumur, so they went to their mirut, split them and made khumur from them." (Narrated by al-Bukhari.)

So the Wise Lawgiver took care of the woman's dress from above, saying: ﴿and let them draw their head-coverings over their chests…﴾, and from below He said: ﴿let them draw their outer garments over themselves…﴾ (33:59).

Then He, Exalted is He, says: ﴿and not display their adornment except to their husbands…﴾: that is, their husbands, since adornment is made for them; ﴿or their fathers…﴾; ﴿or their husbands' fathers…﴾: the husband's father, but if there is fear of temptation from him, the wife should not display her adornment before him.

The meaning of ﴿or their women…﴾ is: the women who work with her in the house, such as maids and servants; ﴿or those whom their right hands possess…﴾: here too the intent is those whom the right hand possesses among women, not men.

It is a condition for these women that they be Muslims. If they are non-believers, like those who are brought in from other countries, it is not permissible for a woman to display her adornment before them, and she should consider them in this matter like men, because they are not Muslims and cannot be trusted with a Muslim woman; perhaps she would go and describe to a non-believing man what she saw of her mistress, and he would become preoccupied with her.

Some scholars hold that those whom the right hand possesses are not restricted to women only, but include men as well, so a woman may display her adornment before them. They said: this is because there is emotional attraction and emotional restraint in the human soul; a servant in the palace does not look at his mistress or her daughters, because he does not aspire to that rank, unless they encourage him and open the door for him, and that is a different matter.

As for His saying: ﴿or male attendants who have no physical desire…﴾: that is, attendants of the household who live on its leftovers, so the life of the attendant is part of the life of his master; he has no house to shelter him, so he sleeps wherever he can, and has no food, so people feed him, and so on. He is lost, with no aim and no independence in his life. You see such people eating the leftovers of tables, wearing rags, and sleeping even on the pavements.

Like the simpleton or the idiot whom people pity, who has no desire for women and does not understand such matters, so one need not fear him with regard to women, because he has no need of them and does not aspire to look at the people of the house.

The meaning of ﴿male attendants who have no physical desire…﴾ is: such as one who is elderly and feeble in strength, having no capacity for these matters, or one who is castrated (majbub), with his organ cut off; there is no danger from such people to women.

As for His saying: ﴿or children who are not yet aware of the private aspects of women…﴾:

We observe here that "tifl" (child) is singular, yet it is described with a plural: ﴿who have not yet become aware of the private aspects of women…﴾. Why? They said: this is a feature of the language, namely precision of expression, whereby the singular word is used to indicate the dual and the plural.

As we say: "this is a just judge," "these two are just judges," "these are just judges"; we do not say "two just ones" or "just ones." When the description is made singular for all without caprice, the description is like one thing: the judge does not judge according to his mood and desire, and another according to his mood and desire, but all proceed from one law and one balance. So justice is one; it is not said to be graded, and there is no separate justice for each of them; justice is one.

Likewise in the case of ﴿al-tifl…﴾: although the intent is children, it says "child" because their instincts are shared with all, and they have no desire of their own; all children, then, are as if they were one child, since no individual mind has yet formed in each of them. All love play and games, and there is nothing beyond that; the plurality here is not evident, because of the unity in their instincts and inclinations.

The proof is that when children grow up and reach the stage of puberty and have desires, thought and inclination, the Qur'an says of them: ﴿and when the children among you reach puberty…﴾ (24:59). Here it looks to the plural, because there is no unity in the early stage of childhood.

Similar to this is His saying: ﴿Has there come to you the story of the honoured guests of Abraham?﴾ (51:24): He described "guest" (dayf), which is singular, with the plural "honoured" (mukramin). That is because "dayf" also indicates the plural: the guest is one who has come upon the house and has rights and obligations which the host must fulfil, beyond what the house needs; and the guest in these obligations is one, whether singular or a group; so the singular indicates the plural.

As for His saying: ﴿who have not yet become aware of the private aspects of women…﴾: "yazharu 'ala" has two meanings in the language. The first: to know, as in His saying: ﴿if they come to know of you, they will stone you…﴾ (18:20), meaning, if they learn of you and recognise your place.

The second: to rise above, prevail and overpower, as in His saying: ﴿so they were not able to scale it (yazharuhu)…﴾ (18:97), meaning the barrier that Dhu al-Qarnayn built: they were not able to climb over it and rise above it.

Here, ﴿who have not yet become aware of the private aspects of women…﴾ means: they do not know them or discern them, or are not able to attain what is sought from them; so they have no knowledge or understanding of these matters.

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And let them not stamp their feet so as to reveal what they hide of their adornment…﴾:

Allah, blessed and exalted, exposes the tricks and stratagems of women in attracting glances. If their appearance does not draw your attention, the sound produced by their gait will: as if she were saying to you, "O you, listen!" In the past, women wore anklets that made a sound when walking; now they put under their shoes something that produces such a sound when walking. The first to use these tricks were dancers, to attract glances to themselves.

It is well known that the manner in which a woman walks reveals much of her adornment that people do not see, and causes much temptation. Therefore He, Exalted is He, says after it, at the conclusion of these matters: ﴿And turn to Allah in repentance, all of you, O believers, so that you may succeed.﴾ (24:31)

Allah, Blessed and Exalted, did not say: "O you who have committed these sins that have been discussed," but rather He said: ﴿all of you﴾, urging everyone to repent, to show that every son of Adam is a sinner; and however committed a Muslim may be, he cannot be sure that some slip will not escape him here or there. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is the Creator and the Most Knowing of whom He created; so He opened for them the door of repentance and urged them towards it, and said to them: "You need only repent, and as for Me, I remain."

It is said: the fool who has no need for women. It is said: the simpleton. It is said: the man who follows a people, eats with them and depends on them, and is weak and does not desire women." Then he said: "All these differences are close in meaning, and they converge on one who has no understanding and no drive by which he takes notice of matters concerning women."

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿And marry off the single among you, and the righteous among your male servants and your female servants. If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty. And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ (24:32)

After the Truth, exalted is He, spoke about the matter of guarding the private parts and called to preserve the purity of lineages, He wished to speak about those men or women for whom the matter of marriage has not been made easy. This is so that the subject is treated from all its aspects, because the Legislator must cover with legislation all the gaps of life and not address one side while leaving the other.

﴿al-Ayama (the single)...﴾ (24:32): the plural of ayyim. An ayyim, among men, is one who has no wife, and an ayyim, among women, is one who has no husband.

We notice that the imperative in ﴿ankihu (marry off)...﴾ (24:32) came thus with the hamzat al-qat' (the initial hamza that is always pronounced), although the imperative to the single person is "unkih" with the hamzat al-wasl (the connecting hamza, dropped when speaking). This is because the command here (ankihu, in the plural) is not addressed to the single individual who will marry the ayyim, but to others that they should marry him or her. The intended meaning is a command to guardians and to those among them who have men without wives or women without husbands: hasten the marriage of these people, make this matter easy for them, and do not be strict about marriage expenses so that you may keep your sons and daughters chaste. And if you do not help them, then at least do not be strict and do not be extravagant.

In the noble hadith: "If one comes to you whose religion and character you are pleased with, then marry him to her. If you do not do so, there will be trial on earth and great corruption."(1)

Nevertheless, in our societies there are many customs and traditions that obstruct the marriage of young people, the most dangerous of which is extravagance in dowries and expenses and looking to outward appearances, etc., as if the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, were saying to the guardians: make easy for the youth the matters of lawful union, and pave for them the path of chastity.

The Qur'an has given us a model of what a guardian should be. He, exalted is He, said of our master Shu'ayb, peace be upon him: ﴿He said, "I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine..."﴾ (28:27). This is because Musa, peace be upon him, would be a hired worker with him, and perhaps he would not aspire to ask for his daughter's hand; so he offered her to him, proposed her to him, and encouraged him to proceed to her marriage, thus removing from him the shyness of hesitation. Thus should the father of the girl be, if he finds a suitable match for his daughter, so that he does not hesitate to grant her chastity.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the righteous among your male servants and your female servants...﴾ (24:32):

And his saying (ṣ): "A woman is married for four things: for her wealth, her beauty, her lineage, and her religion. So win the one with religion; your hands will be rubbed with dust (i.e., you will prosper)."(2)

When al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked about the matter of marriage, he said to the father of the girl who came to consult him: "Marry her to one whom you trust with his religion; if he loves your daughter he will honour her, and if he dislikes her he will not wrong her." And what more does a person want in his daughter's husband than this?

Religion, character and lofty values are the foundation upon which choice is built; as for wealth, it is a secondary thing and a passing accident. Therefore He, exalted is He, says: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty. And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ (24:32)

Poverty may be a cause for a girl not being sought after, or for the girl's family not being inclined to the husband. But how would Allah abandon us when we fear Him and intend chastity and purity? It is not possible that Allah would withhold from a couple who have met upon these values and gathered upon these manners. And who knows, perhaps provision will come to both of them together, and their union in this legitimate bond will be the gate of provision opened for both of them at once?

﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ (24:32): So the giving of Allah is constant and never ceases, for His treasuries are never exhausted nor diminished. A person withholds spending because he fears poverty, but the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, gives abundantly, because what He has never runs out.

(1) Related by al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (1084) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, with the wording "If one whose religion and character you are pleased with proposes to you, then marry him, unless you do so, there will be trial on earth and great corruption." Ibn Majah also related it in his Sunan (1967) with the wording "If one comes to you." Al-Tirmidhi preferred that it is mursal (with a gap in the chain) in the narration of al-Layth ibn Sa'd.

(2) A hadith agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh). Related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (5090) and Muslim in his Sahih (1466), Book of Suckling, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him. Al-Qurtubi said, as quoted from him by Ibn Hajar in Fath al-Bari (9/136): "The meaning of the hadith is that these four qualities are those for which a woman is desired in marriage; it is a report of what exists in reality in this regard, not that a command was issued to that effect. Its apparent meaning is the permissibility of marrying for the purpose of each of these, but seeking religion is preferable."

Then Allah, exalted is He, says:

﴿And let those who find no means to marry keep themselves chaste until Allah enriches them from His bounty. And those of your slaves who seek a deed of manumission, write it for them if you know any good in them, and give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you. And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution, when they desire chastity, in order to seek the transitory gain of worldly life. And whoever compels them - indeed, Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (24:33)

In the case where we do not marry off the unmarried (al-ayama) and do not help them to marry, and they themselves are unable to bear its expenses, the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, describes for them the appropriate remedy, which is abstinence (al-isti'faf). Allah the Exalted has required the Islamic community, whether represented by guardians or by society at large, to take up the matter of the unmarried and to help them marry. If the community does not fulfil its role, and these unmarried persons have no capacity of their own to marry, then each of them should keep himself chaste until Allah enriches him. This shows that the legislation builds its rulings and takes all circumstances into account, whether they all obey or all disobey.

As for His saying, ﴿And let those who find no means... (24:33)﴾: it means he should seek chastity, ask for it, and look for its causes, striving to be chaste. The first of the causes of chastity is that he lowers his gaze when he sees, so that nothing arouses or excites him. If he finds in himself youthful vigour and actual strength, he should bridle it and weaken it by lawful means, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O young men, whoever among you is able to marry (al-ba'ah), meaning the expenses of married life, let him marry; and whoever is not able, let him fast, for it is a shield (wija') for him." (2)

Fasting works to break this desire and calm the fierceness of the instinct, because the fasting person eats only what sustains his body and leaves nothing in his body that arouses desire, as the noble hadith states: "The son of Adam need only a few morsels to keep his back upright..." (3)

Or: the young man should devote himself to beneficial and useful work that occupies him and exhausts his effort and energy, which, if not directed to good, will be directed to evil. Through work the young man establishes his self, trusts himself, and earns what is lawful, which encourages him over time to marry and bear its responsibilities.

Therefore He said, ﴿And let those who find no means... (24:33)﴾ and did not say "and let them be chaste" (wa-ya'uff); the meaning is that he should take the path of chastity for himself and strive toward it, by restraining the arousing sight and calming the fierceness of the instinct through fasting, or by working so that he occupies his time and returns at the end of the day tired, wanting to sleep so that he rises in the morning energetic for his work; thus he finds no opportunity for anything that angers Allah.

The meaning of ﴿those who find no means to marry... (24:33)﴾ is: they have no capacity within themselves nor help from their community.

His saying, ﴿until Allah enriches them from His bounty... (24:33)﴾, indicates that chastity is a means of gaining richness, because chastity arises only from the will for piety, and Allah has said in a Qur'anic principle: "And whoever fears Allah - He will make for him a way out (2) and provide for him from where he does not expect (3)" (65:2-3). From this door comes the wealth of Allah to him.

Then the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, says: ﴿And those of your slaves who seek a deed of manumission, write it for them if you know any good in them, and give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you... (24:33)﴾:

Al-kitab: it is well known as the gathering of several written things on paper, and what is meant here is the contract of manumission (al-mukatabah), which is that you write a contract between yourself and the enslaved servant, stipulating that he works for you such-and-such, after which he becomes free if he fulfils what is stated in the manumission contract.

﴿Write it for them if you know any good in them... (24:33)﴾: meaning, if their freedom will lead to good, such as lifting from them the humiliation of slavery and making them active in life with an activity suited to their talents.

Therefore the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, made this manumission one of the channels of zakat, saying: ﴿and for the freeing of slaves... (2:177)﴾: meaning the slaves whom we wish to free from the captivity and humiliation of slavery through emancipation. Although zakat money is given to the poor and the needy, etc., in "the freeing of slaves" the money is given to the master so that he may free his slave.

Just as Islam made the freeing of slaves an expiation for some sins between the slave and his Lord, because Allah wishes to end this matter.

﴿And give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you... (24:33)﴾:

The Truth, blessed and exalted is He, is the Provider, and wealth in reality belongs to Allah. But if He has made you its owner and asks you to give it to your poor brother, He respects your ownership and does not take back the gift to you. Therefore He takes the charity from you as though it were a loan that the poor man does not repay; rather your Lord, mighty and majestic, takes charge of repaying it, so He says: ﴿Who is it that would loan Allah a goodly loan... (2:245)﴾, and He did not say "lend to so-and-so", but "lend to Allah", because He, exalted is He, is the Creator, and it is the right of His servant whom He summoned into existence that He provide for him and undertake his sustenance.

Respect for ownership makes a person confident that the effects of his life's activity and the fruit of his effort will return to him; otherwise what would be the reason to work and exert effort if its fruit were lost and its owner deprived of it? Then many interests would be disrupted and the individual would work only to the extent of his need, so nothing would overflow from him for charity.

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution, when they desire chastity, in order to seek the transitory gain of worldly life. And whoever compels them - indeed, Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving and Merciful. (24:33)﴾:

The male slave is called fata (young man), and the female slave fatah (young woman). The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade a man to say "my slave" (abdi) and "my female slave" (amati); rather he should say "my young man" (fataya) and "my young woman" (fatati). This designation is more honourable and higher for them; fata derives from futuwwah and strength, as if you were saying: "this is my strength which supports me and helps me in the affairs of life." The Prophet (ﷺ) wished to raise their status.

Among these were the group of Mamluks who ruled Egypt at one time, and they were from the sons of kings, sultans and notables.

Prostitution was a phenomenon that Islam found widespread. A man who owned a group of female slaves would set up a banner to identify them, the young men would come to them, and he would collect the price. Among these was Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, the head of hypocrisy, who had (Musaykah and Mu'adhah), and this verse was revealed concerning him (5).

The interpretation of the verse: do not compel the slave women to prostitution, while they were weeping and refusing this act; they were harmed, subjected to insult and slander, and people dared to approach them. Among these slave women were girls of good and noble origin, but fate led them to captivity in wars or otherwise, whereas the free chaste woman walks without anyone harming her.

The meaning of ﴿when they desire chastity... (24:33)﴾: the Qur'an speaks here of the reality, so that if they do not desire chastity, do not compel them. ﴿in order to seek the transitory gain of worldly life... (24:33)﴾: seeking a little passing wealth. ﴿And whoever compels them - indeed, Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving and Merciful (24:33)﴾: because in a case of compulsion to prostitution they lose the condition of choice, so they do not bear the sin of this crime, in accordance with the noble prophetic hadith: "Allah has overlooked for my community error, forgetting, and what they are compelled to do." (6)

Therefore the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, reassures those women who desire protection and chastity but whose master compels them to prostitution and forces them by any means: be assured, there is no sin upon you in this case, and Allah will forgive you, for Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.

1 Al-wija': it is that the two testicles are struck with a severe blow that removes the desire for intercourse, so that he becomes like a eunuch. Ibn Manzur said in [Lisan al-Arab, root wja'a] that he meant fasting cuts off marriage as the wija' cuts it off.
2 A hadith agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh). Related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (5065), and Muslim in his Sahih (1400), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud may Allah be pleased with him.
3 Related by Ahmad in his Musnad (4/132), and al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (2380), from the hadith of al-Miqdam ibn Ma'dikarib, and its complete text: "No son of Adam fills a vessel worse than his belly. It is enough for the son of Adam to have a few morsels to keep his back upright; if he must, then a third for his food, a third for his drink, and a third for his breath."
4 From Abu Hurayrah may Allah be pleased with him, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "None of you should say: Feed your Lord, water your Lord. Let him say: my master (sayyidi), my lord (mawlaya). And none of you should say: my slave (abdi), my female slave (amati); let him say: my young man (fataya), my young woman (fatati), and my boy (ghulami)." Related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (2552), and Muslim in his Sahih (2249), Book of Etiquette (al-Alfaz min al-Adab).
5 Al-Zuhri said: there was a slave girl of Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul called Mu'adhah, whom he compelled to fornication; when Islam came, ﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution... (24:33)﴾ was revealed. Related by al-Bazzar in his Musnad (cited by Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir 3/288). And from Jabir, who said: it was revealed concerning a slave girl of Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul called Musaykah, whom he compelled to immorality, and she was not bad, but she refused, so Allah revealed this verse ﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution... (24:33)﴾. Related by al-A'mash.
6 Its meaning is related by Ibn Majah in his Sunan (2045), al-Daraqutni in his Sunan (4/170), and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak (2/198), who declared it sahih according to the conditions of al-Bukhari and Muslim, from Ibn Abbas, with the wording: "Allah has overlooked for my community: error, forgetting, and what they are compelled to do." See also Kashf al-Khafa (1/522).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 24, verse 34:

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear signs, and an example from those who passed away before you, and an admonition for the God-fearing.﴾

The meaning: There is no excuse for you, for Allah, exalted is He, has sent down to you clear signs which guarantee for you the honour of life, its purity, and the purity of the lineage of the vicegerent of Allah on earth. These signs have left nothing of the affairs of life untouched without addressing it and laying down the ruling on it. Were there in your life some matter or issue that legislation had not addressed and had not organized, we might seek an excuse for you.

Therefore our master, the Imam ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said about the Qur'an: "In it is the judgement of what is among you, the news of what came before you, and the report of what will come after you. It is the decisive word, not a jest. Whoever abandons it from a tyrant, Allah will break him; and whoever seeks guidance in other than it, Allah will lead him astray."(1)

Time does not cease to confirm the truth of this saying. Look here and there and you will find the downfall of the opinions, doctrines, parties and states that rose to contradict Islam, whether they were fierce capitalism or fierce communism, etc. All of them collapsed before the eyes and ears of everyone.

Yes: whoever abandons it from a tyrant, Allah will break him; and whoever seeks guidance in other than it, Allah will lead him astray. This is because He is your Creator, and He knows best what sets you right. It is therefore not fitting for you, then, to take the creation of Allah for yourself and then act arrogantly toward Him, setting for yourself a law of your own devising.

We have previously said that the word "signs" (āyāt) is used in three senses: the cosmic signs which draw your attention to the Creator, the Originator, exalted is He; the miracles which come to establish the truthfulness of the Messenger in conveying from Allah; and the signs bearing the rulings, which are the verses of the noble Qur'an. And in the Qur'an all of this is found.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and an example from those who passed away before you, and an admonition for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Nur]:

That is: We have made for you an admonition and a lesson through the nations before you, which reached the peak of civilization, yet they did not possess the foundations of survival, and did not produce for themselves the immunity that would protect them, so they collapsed. Nothing remains of them but traces such as those we see now of the ancient Egyptians, who attained a level of civilization that astonished the advanced modern world, so people now come marvelling: how did the ancient Egyptians achieve this civilization?

Greater than the civilization of the Pharaohs was the civilization of ʿAd, about which Allah said: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with ʿAd, [with] Iram of the pillars, the like of which had not been created in the lands?﴾ [al-Fajr] — meaning: it had no equal in the world — ﴿and Thamud, who carved out the rocks in the valley, and Pharaoh, owner of the stakes, who transgressed in the lands and increased corruption therein? So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment. Indeed, your Lord is ever in observation.﴾ [al-Fajr] — meaning: none of the transgressors will escape, and no disbeliever will be saved from the punishment of Allah.

The same applies to the matter of adultery and the slander of chaste, virtuous women, like the incident of the slander (al-ifk) which was discussed earlier, and which was an example and a lesson. Likewise the story of Lady Mary was an example, when her people accused her and said: ﴿O sister of Aaron, your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother an unchaste woman.﴾ [Maryam]

Likewise was the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the wife of the chief minister (al-ʿAziz), all of them matters concerning honour, and they did not lack the slandering of chaste, virtuous women, or of the pure, chaste Yusuf son of Yaʿqub, peace be upon them both.

These signs are clear manifestations of the Supreme Existence in the signs of the cosmos; clear proofs of the truthfulness of the one who conveys from Allah through the miracles; and clear explanations of the rulings which organize the movement of life in the verses of the Qur'an. Then We showed them the outcome of the earlier nations, whether those who turned to Allah in obedience or those who turned away from Him in disobedience. None benefits from these admonitions and lessons except the God-fearing, who fear Allah and in whom the admonition bears fruit.

1 Cited by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir (3/289).

Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 24, verse 35:

﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. His light is like a niche within which is a lamp, the lamp is within a glass, the glass is as if it were a glittering star, lit from a blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it. Light upon light. Allah guides to His light whom He wills. And Allah presents parables for the people, and Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾ (24:35)

We say: Allah, exalted is He, has given us sensory light by which we see the forms of things, and He has made it a means to the non-sensory light. We have said that when the world grows dark, each of us lights up for himself according to his capacity and ability to illuminate. But when the sun rises and Allah illumines the universe, each of us extinguishes his light, because the light of Allah is sufficient. Just as the light of Allah is sufficient in sensory matters, so His light is also sufficient in non-sensory matters.

So when Allah legislates a non-sensory ruling that organizes the movement of life, beware lest you oppose it with something of your own. Just as you extinguished physical lamps before His lamp, extinguish your non-sensory lamps likewise before His rulings and commands, exalted is He. The matter is clear in the cosmic signs.

﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth…﴾ (24:35). As we say, and to Allah belongs the highest likeness: "So-and-so is the light of the house." The verse does not make Allah known to us; rather, it makes us know His effect upon us. He, glorified is He, is the illuminer of the heavens and the earth, and they are the widest thing we can imagine, such that everything in them is clear and not hidden.

Then our Lord, Mighty and Majestic, gives us an illustrative parable of His light, saying: ﴿like a niche within which is a lamp…﴾ (24:35). That is: like His illumination of the heavens and the earth. ﴿Like a niche…﴾ (24:35): this is the recess that they used to make in the wall in ancient times, a non-penetrating hollow in which they placed the lamp or the oil-lamp, so this hollow holds the light and gathers it in one direction, so that it becomes strong, and it casts no shadow in the path of the light.

The lamp (miṣbāḥ) is a small vessel into which oil or, later, kerosene is placed, and in its middle is a wick that draws up the oil so that it remains burning. If the wick is left in the open air, the air toys with it, scatters its light and produces smoke, because it takes from the air more than what combustion requires. Therefore they placed a glass barrier around the wick to keep the air away from it, so that the light comes forth clear, without smoke in it. They used to call this soot (al-hibāb).

Thus the lamp evolved into a bulb, its light rose and its efficiency increased. Among this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the lamp is within a glass…﴾ (24:35). But it is not an ordinary glass; it is ﴿as if it were a glittering star…﴾ (24:35). That is: a star of pearl, and pearl shines by itself.

Likewise its oil is not ordinary oil; it is the oil of a blessed olive tree.

The Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿lit from a blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west…﴾ (24:35). That is: the olive tree is neither of the east nor of the west; that is, not of the east, because it is of the west, and not of the west, because it is of the east. It is therefore both east and west alike. But how is that?

They said: because the olive tree, when it is in the east, the west is dark, and when it is in the west, the east is dark. Thus light and darkness would come upon it; but this one is neither eastern nor western, rather it is eastern-western, nothing blocks its light from it.

This affects its oil, so you see it in its clarity and brilliance ﴿whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it﴾ (24:35). The tree gives strong light that fits its kinship to the sun. If the sun is what illumines the world, then the olive tree is its daughter, and from it she draws her light, so that the sunlight never leaves her.

So: the illumination of Allah of the heavens and the earth is like this complete niche as we described. Look at a niche with a lamp of these specifications: would there be any dark place in it? The heavens and the earth, for all their vastness, are like this niche. The parable here is not for the light of Allah itself; it is for His illumination of the heavens and the earth. As for His light, exalted is He, it is something else, beyond description. The parable here is only to bring the matter closer to minds.

We have already mentioned the story of Abu Tammam when he described the caliph and praised him with the most prominent qualities among the Arabs. He said:
"The boldness of ʿAmr with the generosity of Ḥātim,
the forbearance of al-Aḥnaf with the intelligence of Iyās."
He thus gathered for the caliph all these qualities and praised him with the most famous traits among the Arabs. Therefore one of the envious rose against him and objected: "How do you liken the caliph to the vagabonds of the Arabs? The prince is above those you have described."

Abu Tammam immediately completed it, in the same meter and rhyme:
"Do not deny my striking for him a parable beyond Him,
wandering in generosity and courage.
For Allah has struck for Him, beneath Him, the most exalted parable for His light:
from the niche and the lamp."

So Allah, blessed and exalted is He, is the light of the heavens and the earth, that is, their illuminer. This is very clear when you look at the light of the sun at the hour it appears and lights up the universe, such that no other light appears with it, and the lights of the other planets and stars fade, despite their existence alongside the sun at the same time; their light is overcome by the light of the sun. As the poet said in praise:
"You are like the sun, and the kings are like stars;
when they appear, no star is seen among them."

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿light upon light…﴾ (24:35). The Truth, glorified and exalted is He, did not leave us with sensory light only; rather He sent us another light through the messengers, the light of the method that organizes the movement of life for us. As if He, exalted is He, were saying: "I have sent you light upon light: sensory light and moral, non-sensory light. If you witness that My sensory light illumines the heavens and the earth for you, and when it appears all your lights vanish before it, then know that My light of method likewise overcomes all your methods, and you have no right to adopt the methods of men while the method of Allah exists."

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah guides to His light whom He wills…﴾ (24:35): that is, to His non-sensory light, the light of the method and the light of the obligations. The disbelievers did not attain this light, even though they attained the sensory light of the sun and the moon and benefited from it, and extinguished their lamps before it; but they had no portion of the non-sensory light, for they shut their eyes, their hearts and their ears against it, so they did not benefit from it.

They should have understood that the non-sensory light of Allah, like His sensory light, cannot be dispensed with. Therefore there came in a report from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib: "Whoever abandons it from a tyrant, Allah breaks him; and whoever seeks guidance in other than it, Allah misguides him."

Wondrously, the more the servant delves into guidance, the more he increases in light upon light, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿O you who have believed, if you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion…﴾ (8:29).

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety.﴾ (47:17)

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And Allah presents parables for the people…﴾ (24:35): that is, for admonition and instruction, like the previous parable of His light, ﴿and Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ (24:35).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 24, verse 36:

﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised, and in which His name is remembered; therein glorify Him in the mornings and the evenings.﴾

The verse begins with the prepositional phrase ﴿in houses…﴾ (al-Nur: 36), and we must seek for it something it depends on (muta'alliq). The meaning is: this light that was previously mentioned is [found] in houses which Allah has permitted to be raised.

The bayt (house) is that which is prepared for spending the night, or rather for the settled living of life, and to it a person retreats after the toil of the day and his wandering through the expanses of the earth. A house, in whatever form, is a person's private place which isolates him from the general society and gives him a distinctiveness in himself; otherwise a person would not be content to live in a public square with other people.

This privacy in houses varies among people and rises according to their capacities, and every person wants to withdraw into a place specific to him, because withdrawal (tahayyuz) is something desired in the human soul. The family wants to withdraw from general society, and the individuals within the family also want to withdraw, each to a room that belongs to him. The same applies to clothing, for each of us has private matters between himself and himself that he does not like anyone to see.

Allah has taken for Himself a house on earth, the first house established for people, as the Truthful, Glorified and Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed…﴾ (Al 'Imran: 96). This is the House of Allah by the choice of Allah. Then the houses of Allah multiplied, which the creation of Allah chose. Just as you have taken houses for yourselves, Allah has taken houses for Himself: ﴿[in houses] which Allah has permitted to be raised and in which His name is remembered…﴾ (al-Nur: 36).

You are all servants of Allah and the dependants of Allah, and you will find rest in His house, exalted is He, just as you find rest in your houses, with the difference between rest in your house and rest in the House of Allah.

Rest in your houses is sensory, physical rest in a comfortable lounge or a kitchen full of food; but in the House of Allah the rest is spiritual and of value, because your Lord, mighty and majestic, is unseen, and so He grants you rest also in an unseen way.

Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) whenever a matter distressed him would stand to the prayer (salah) (1) to cast his burdens upon his Lord. And what do you say about a craft (sun'ah) that is presented to its maker once a day: would any defect or corruption remain in it? So what of you, if it is presented to its maker five times in the day and night?

So your Lord calls you to His house to give you rest, to lift from you your worries, to correct what has become corrupted in you, and to open for you the doors of relief. Thus, "light upon light" is only found in the houses of Allah which He, glorified is He, has permitted to be raised by remembrance and acts of obedience, and which are elevated above what takes place in other places and are magnified.

All houses are of one level, but some houses are raised above others and exalted; the houses of Allah have been raised by obedience and worship. The mosque is a place of worship in which Allah is never disobeyed at all, unlike houses and other places. So Allah magnified His houses above being disobeyed in them, and magnified their frequenters above occupying themselves in them with the base worldly affairs of life. So you must leave the world at the door of the mosque, just as you leave your shoe.

Therefore Islam forbade us to conclude a sale (safqah) in the House of Allah, or even to announce a lost item in it, because the transaction concluded in the House of Allah is ruinous and destructive, and the lost item announced in it by its owner will not be returned to him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded us to say to one who does this: "May Allah not return it to you." (2)

Although Allah has made the whole earth a mosque and a means of purification for the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), there is a difference between praying in the mosque and praying in any other place. The mosque is designated for worship, and in it we mention none but Allah, whereas other places are suitable for prayer and also for carrying out the affairs of this world.

Otherwise, how is it that you live your whole time for the affairs of this world throughout the day and night, and then begrudge your Lord these minutes in which you perform the obligation Allah has imposed on you, dragging the world along with you even into the House of Allah? Do you not know that the houses of Allah were only made for the worship of Allah? A believer must leave his worldly life outside the mosque, and intend to devote himself to i'tikaf (seclusion) in the worship of his Lord and to persistence in His remembrance in His house. It is not fitting for you to be in the House of Allah and to be occupied with other than Him.

If you adhere to the etiquette of the mosque, you will receive from your Lord light upon light, the burden and grief will be removed from your shoulders, and your problems will be resolved from where you do not expect.

So the Truthful, Blessed and Exalted, placed in the natural disposition (fitrah) of faith that you believe in a god; faith is a natural matter, however much a person tries to deny it. The disbeliever who denies the existence of Allah, at the moment he is struck by a crisis from which there is no escape by human means, you will find him spontaneously turning to Allah, saying: "O Lord!" He cannot lie to himself in this state, nor surrender himself and sell it cheaply.

On this the Exalted says: ﴿And when harm touches the man, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance. Then when He grants him a favor from Him, he forgets that for which he had been calling upon Him before, and sets up rivals to Allah…﴾ (al-Zumar: 8).

Among the precision of the Qur'anic expression in this matter is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, when the call is made for prayer on the day of Jumu'ah, then hasten to the remembrance of Allah and leave off trade…﴾ (al-Jumu'ah: 9).

He mentioned one side of the process of trade, which is selling (bay'), and did not say "and buying" (shira'). They said: because when selling is prohibited, buying is prohibited at the same time; and because a person is eager for selling but may buy while disliking it, so a person's desire is attached to selling, not buying, since buying requires money from him, unlike selling which brings him money.

So the saying of the Exalted: ﴿and leave off trade…﴾ (al-Jumu'ah: 9) mentions only the peak and essence of the movement of life, for all the movements of life, whether trade, agriculture or industry, end in the matter of selling. Therefore the seller grieves when he does not sell, whereas the buyer, when he does not find the item or finds the shop closed, says: "Blessing, O gatherer!"

Then when the prayer has ended, He brings us back again to the movement of life: ﴿And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse within the land and seek of the bounty of Allah…﴾ (al-Jumu'ah: 10).

It is as if you went to the mosque to take a charge of faith that helps you and governs all your senses in your movement in trade, in production, in consumption, and in everything that benefits you and develops your life. When your Lord commands you to devote yourself to performing the prayer, He does not want this leisure to disable the movement of your life; rather, He wants to give you the necessary fuel so that the movement of your life becomes in accordance with what Allah wills. This time which we set aside from the interests of our worldly life for the worship of Allah is like charging a battery: when you take the battery to the charging device, we do not say that you have disabled the battery; rather you have increased its capacity to perform its task and to draw its benefit.

So you go to the House of Allah with the light of faith and with the light of responding to the call: Allahu Akbar, and you come out with multiple lights from the outpourings of Allah. Therefore the Truthful, Blessed and Exalted struck for us a parable of this light with a lamp whose light grows and rises, because it is in a glass that increases its brightness, since it is like a shining star, and the light rises because it is from the oil of an olive tree, and it rises because it is both eastern and western at once. So there are many colours in the parable, and likewise is the light in the houses of Allah.

Therefore some of the knowers (ʿarifun) said: the people of the earth look up at the sky and see shining stars, while the angels in the sky look and see shining stars from the houses of Allah. There is no wonder in this, for these are the lights of Allah shining and flowing in His house and in His mosque. And how do we deem this unlikely, when we see how the light of the sun, when it is reflected on the surface of the moon, sends down to us the light that we see? The sun and the moon are a trace of the traces of the light of Allah which shines in the houses of Allah. Does that radiance, which surpasses the radiance of the full moons, not give us that?

Then He, the Exalted, says: ﴿glorifying Him therein in the mornings and the evenings﴾ (al-Nur: 36). The mosques were made for the glorification of Allah; therefore some of the righteous, when they arrived in a town, would contrive to enter it at a time other than the prayer, then go to the mosque; if they found it populated at a time other than prayer by those glorifying Allah, they knew that these were committed to the way of Allah, since they sit before the time of prayer glorifying Allah and awaiting the prayer; and if they found the situation otherwise, they turned away from it and knew it was a town with no good in it. (5)

Al-ghuduww means the morning, and al-aasal means the evening; they are never free of the remembrance of Allah and His glorification.

2 From Abu Hurayrah (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu), who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If you see someone selling or buying in the mosque, say: May Allah not make your trade profitable; and if you see someone announcing a lost item, say: May Allah not return it to you." Narrated by al-Nasa'i in ʿAmal al-Yawm wa al-Layla (p. 73), al-Darimi in his Sunan (1/326), and al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (1321), who said: hasan gharib.

4 There is another reading, "yusabbaḥu," recited by ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim in the narration of Abu Bakr from him, and al-Hasan, with a fatha on the ba' in the passive form. Mentioned by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (6/4812).
5 al-Qurtubi mentioned in his tafsir (6/4812): "Salim ibn ʿAbd Allah saw the people of the markets coming to the prayer, and said: these are the ones whom Allah meant by His saying ﴿men whom neither trade nor sale distracts from the remembrance of Allah…﴾ (al-Nur: 37). Then he said: The scholars differed regarding the description by Allah of those who glorify Him. It was said: they are those who watch over the command of Allah, seeking His pleasure, whom nothing of the affairs of this world distracts from the prayer and the remembrance of Allah."

Al-Sha'rawi, commentary on surah 24, verse 37:

Allah describes those who maintain the houses of Allah with remembrance and glorification as: "Men whom neither trade nor sale distracts from the remembrance of Allah, the establishment of the prayer, and the giving of zakah. They fear a Day when hearts and eyes will be turned about." (24:37)

We say: trade is the very heart of the movement of life, for it is the intermediary between the producer, whether a farmer or a craftsman, and the consumer. It involves buying and selling, which are the core of all exchange. These men were not distracted from the remembrance of Allah by trade, because they knew the blessing that lies in the time set aside for prayer, a blessing that spreads throughout the remaining time.

Or we say: trade did not distract them from the remembrance of Allah in itself. While trading, they did not neglect the remembrance of Allah. When we were young, we used to hear in the markets, between the seller and the buyer, one of them saying to the other: "Glorify Allah," "Invoke blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ)," "Praise the Prophet (ﷺ)," "With the invoking of blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ)." All these expressions have now disappeared from the markets and commercial dealings. In their place have come other values and phrases that depend on display and advertising, and even deception and fraud. We no longer hear these expressions. Indeed, if a sale did not take place, you would hear the seller say: "We have gained the blessing of invoking blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ)," for it is in itself a gain even if no sale is made.

﴿And the establishment of the prayer and the giving of zakah...﴾ (An-Nur 24:37): As for the prayer, it takes up time from one's work, and a person often becomes preoccupied with his work and trade, neglecting the establishment of the prayer, thinking that it will waste his time and cause him to miss many interests. Likewise, people regard zakah as diminishing their wealth. This is a mistaken and foolish view, because the farmer who takes an ardab (a dry measure) of wheat out of his storehouse to sow his land: the fool says, "The storehouse has been reduced by an ardab," whereas the wise person is confident that this ardab will multiply many times over at the harvest.

Or: Allah, exalted is He, bestows upon him from His lights, so He blesses his time for him, and he accomplishes in the remaining time what one who abandons the prayer cannot accomplish. Or He provides him with a profitable deal that comes to him within minutes, from where he does not expect. Blessing, as we have said, may be negative or positive, and all of these are lights and manifestations that Allah bestows upon the one who is committed to His method.

Then He, glorified is He, says about the attributes of these men: ﴿They fear a Day when hearts and eyes will be turned about.﴾ (An-Nur 24:37) This is because they trade for a loftier and more enduring goal. The people of this world trade only to preserve their worldly life, whereas these men trade with Allah in a commerce that will never fail, a commerce that preserves both this world and the Hereafter.

If you measure the time of your worldly life against the time of your next life, you will find the former to be vanity with no value, just as it is a presumed time for a presumed lifespan, and you do not know when death may surprise you in it. As for the Hereafter, it is a certain, abiding, everlasting life. In this world, pleasure escapes you however sweet and long it may be, whereas the pleasures of the Hereafter are everlasting and never cease.

Therefore, they work for the Hereafter. ﴿They fear a Day when hearts and eyes will be turned about.﴾ (An-Nur 24:37) The Day itself is not what is feared; rather, what occurs in it is feared. Just as a student says, "I feared the day of the examination," though the day is an ordinary day that is not itself feared; what is feared is what will happen on that day. So the meaning is: they fear the punishment of this Day.

The meaning of ﴿hearts and eyes will be turned about﴾ (An-Nur 24:37) is: the trembling of the heart and the agitation of its movement, and the intense pounding that befalls it. We see what befalls hearts of this kind merely from the events of this world, so what of the terror of the Hereafter and the agitation that occurs in the heart then?

Likewise, eyes are agitated and turn here and there, because when they see the terror that frightens them, they turn, looking here and there, perhaps they will see something that reassures them or lightens what they are suffering. But alas, they will see nothing except another terror, even greater and more painful.

Therefore the situation ends with: ﴿Their eyes will be humbled...﴾ (Al-Qalam 68:43), and ﴿Hearts that Day will be trembling, their eyes humbled.﴾ (An-Nazi'at 79:8–9). That is: humiliated and broken, for there is no escape and no refuge. No one will find rest on that Day except the one who sent forward righteous deeds, like the diligent student who is confident in himself and his knowledge, eager for the question paper, whereas the other stands bewildered, not knowing.

(1) A metaphor for bewilderment, extreme terror, and the search for a place of escape from the horrors of the Day of Resurrection (al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/129). It has also been said: they vacillate between hope for salvation and fear of destruction, and the eyes look in every direction, toward where their books will be given to them and toward where they will be taken (Tafsir al-Qurtubi 6/4817).

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿That Allah may reward them with the best of what they did, and increase them of His bounty. And Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning.﴾ [24:38]

That is: on this Day, Allah will reward them with the best of what they did. How wondrous is the mercy of Allah! But how about the worst of what they did? Leave that to the mercy of Allah and His forgiveness. ﴿And increase them of His bounty…﴾ [24:38]: because Allah, exalted is He, does not deal with us in good deeds according to strict justice, nor does He recompense us for them with the perfectly balanced scale and in proportion to what we deserve; rather, He increases us of His bounty.

Therefore it has been related in supplication: "O Allah, deal with us by bounty, not by justice, and by benevolence, not by the balance." There is no salvation for us except by this, as He, glorified is He, says: ﴿Say: "In the bounty of Allah and in His mercy—in that let them rejoice; it is better than what they accumulate."﴾ [10:58]

﴿And Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾ [24:38]: Provision (rizq) is everything from which one benefits, and every meaning that carries an element of excellence for you is provision. So health is provision, knowledge is provision, forbearance is provision, courage is provision… etc.

Some people think that provision means wealth, and this is an error; for provision is a collection of many things. If your provision is knowledge, then teach the ignorant; if your provision is strength, then help the weak; if your provision is forbearance, then be patient with the foolish; and if your provision is a craft you excel at, then make it for the one who is clumsy and cannot do anything well.

So all of this is provision. And since your Lord, mighty and majestic, provides for you without reckoning and pours out upon you of His bounty, then give to the needy, and provide, you too, for the destitute. Know that you are an intermediary from Allah, and that provision originally belongs to Allah, who has guaranteed it to His servants; you are only the outstretched hand of Allah in giving. Know that as long as you are an intermediary in giving, you are giving from treasuries that never run out, so do not be stingy or miserly, for what you have will run out, but what is with Allah endures.

Reckoning (ḥisāb) means calculating the fruit of actions: "This yields such-and-such, that produces such-and-such"—that is, a budget and a feasibility study. But Allah's giving comes to you without these calculations. You calculate because there is someone behind you who will hold you to account; but your Lord, mighty and majestic, is not held to account by anyone. Therefore He gives you without work, without causes, without preliminaries, and gives you while you do not deserve it. Do you not see the one whose foot stumbles and finds beneath it a treasure?

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 24, verse 39:

Then the Truth, glorified be He, says:

﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level desert, which the thirsty one thinks is water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing, and finds Allah with him, and He pays him his account in full. And Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾

Al-Haqq, blessed and exalted is He, wishes to draw the attention of those whom worldly life has occupied with its movement and activity away from what is intended in the Hereafter. They perform many kinds of good deeds, but they did not sincerely intend them for Allah, whereas the basis of doing good is that it should come from Allah and be for Allah. These people will be confronted with this reality, and it will be said to one of them, as came in the hadith: "You fought so that it might be said, and it has been said" (1).

They praised you and lauded you, erected statues for you and immortalised your memory; therefore the Qur'an drew for them this image: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level desert, which the thirsty one thinks is water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing...﴾ (al-Nur).

﴿Their deeds...﴾ (al-Nur): that is, the deeds they consider to be good, and whose reward they expect. The sarab (mirage) is what appears in the desert at midday, as if it were water, and it is not so. This phenomenon is the result of the refraction of light. And qī'a (qay'a) is the plural of qā', which is level land, like jār and jīrah (neighbour and neighbourhood).

The verb ﴿yahsabuhu...﴾ (al-Nur) is attributed to al-zham'an (the thirsty one), because he is in need of water; perhaps, had he not been thirsty, he would not have paid attention to this appearance. Because of his thirst he runs after the water, but he finds nothing. Would that the matter ended at the disappointment of his effort! Rather, ﴿and finds Allah with him, and He pays him his account in full...﴾ (al-Nur): he is confronted with a God who was not on his mind when he did the good, a God in whom he did not believe. Only now does he become aware, awaken from his heedlessness, and find his deed lost.

Thus two calamities gather upon him: the calamity of thirst for which he found no relief, and the calamity of the punishment that awaits him, as the poet said (2):
As a cloud flashed for a people who were thirsty, then when they saw it, it dispersed and vanished (3).

We have previously given an example of this matter: a prisoner whose thirst reached its limit, so he asked for water; the guard brought it to him, and when he put the cup to his mouth and the poor man was eager to drink, the guard spilled the cup. This is called "despair after raising hopes."

Therefore the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, gives us examples in the universe that make people averse to working for people in order to please people, for work for people must be for the sake of Allah. In reality you encounter one who denies a favour and disowns it after you have done him good, and that is only because you acted for his sake; you found the just recompense so that you learn manners and do not work for people afterwards. Had you done what you did for the sake of Allah, you would have found the reward and recompense from Allah before you finished doing that act.

In another place, the Truth, glorified be He, likens the one who spends his wealth to be seen by people to a smooth rock that receives no benefit from water, so nothing grows on it: ﴿The likeness of one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day is like a smooth rock with a little soil upon it; a heavy rain strikes it and leaves it bare. They have no power over anything they have earned. And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾ (al-Baqarah 264).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾ (al-Nur): beware of deeming death and resurrection far off, for the time after death until the Hour is established is a time that is not counted, because it passes over you without your feeling it, as He, glorified be He, said: ﴿As if they had not remained but an evening or its morning.﴾ (al-Nazi'at 46).

Allah the Exalted has concealed the causes and the appointed time of death, for vagueness may be the greatest clarity. By the vagueness of death you remain mindful of it and active for the Hereafter, because you expect it at any moment; it is constantly in your mind, and who knows, perhaps if you lower your gaze you will not raise it again. On this basis the reckoning is near and swift; therefore they said: whoever dies, his resurrection has come.(7)

(1) Related by Muslim in his Sahih (1905), Ahmad in his Musnad (2/322), and al-Nasa'i in his Sunan (6/23, 24), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, in which: "The first of people to be judged on the Day of Resurrection will be a man who was martyred. He will be brought and his blessings will be made known to him, and he will recognise them. He will be asked: What did you do with them? He will say: I fought for You until I was martyred. He will be told: You lie, but you fought so that it would be said, 'He is brave,' and it has been said. Then he will be ordered to be dragged on his face until he is thrown into the Fire." The hadith...
(2) He is Kuthayyir ibn 'Abd al-Rahman Abu Sakhr al-Khuza'i, known as "Kuthayyir 'Azzah," after 'Azzah bint Jamil al-Dumriyyah.
