Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 24, verse 56:

﴿And establish the prayer, and give the zakah, and obey the Messenger, that you may receive mercy.﴾

The Qur'an always pairs these two pillars, and zakah comes after prayer. That is because prayer is the only pillar that was enjoined directly by Allah, whereas the rest of the pillars were enjoined through revelation. We have given an example of this, and to Allah belongs the highest likeness: a leader who assigns a subordinate a task by memorandum or by telephone, but if the matter is important, he summons the competent employee to his office and assigns him the task in person because of its importance.

Likewise, the Truth, blessed and exalted, has commanded all the legal obligations through revelation, except prayer. He enjoined it upon the Messenger of Allah after summoning him to the journey of the Mi'raj (Ascension), and he assigned it to him directly, face to face, without any intermediary. Because of Allah's knowledge of the Prophet's (ﷺ) love for his ummah, He said to him: "I have made prayer obligatory upon you through nearness, and likewise I make it for the one who prays on earth through nearness. If he enters the mosque, he will find Me."

Although the pillars of Islam are five, the testimony of faith and prayer are the two pillars that never leave the believer under any circumstances. You may fail to meet the conditions of fasting, zakah or hajj, so they are not obligatory upon you. Prayer, moreover, is the obligation repeated throughout the day and night, five times, and through it the declaration of loyalty to Allah is constantly made. Allah, glorified be He, distributed it over time so that the believer remains in constant connection with his Lord: whenever worldly affairs occupy him, he finds "Allahu Akbar" calling out to him.

Consider the greatness of the Creator, may He be exalted, when He asks His creation to meet Him and present itself to Him five times each day. He is the One who requests this meeting and makes it obligatory upon you for your own benefit. Can you imagine a made thing presented to its maker five times a day that could suffer a defect?

Your Lord is the One who calls you and invites you to meet Him, and He says: "Allah does not tire until you tire" (1). Out of His mercy toward you and His love for you, He has left you free to choose the time and the place, and He has left you free to end the meeting whenever you wish. If you wish to remain in His house and in His presence, then welcome and abundance are yours.

Because of the importance and status of prayer in Islam, all the pillars of Islam are gathered in it. In prayer the testimony is repeated: "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." In prayer there is zakah, because zakah is a branch of work, work is a branch of time, and prayer takes up time itself. In it there is fasting, since in prayer you refrain from what you refrain from in fasting, and even more. In it there is hajj, because in your prayer you face the Ka'bah.

Thus prayer stands in for all the pillars in perseverance. That is why it is the pillar of the religion, and it is never dropped from the believer under any circumstances. Even if he cannot pray standing, he prays sitting or lying down, and even if he can only gesture with his finger or his eyes, or merely bring it to mind, because the continuity of loyalty is through worship of the Worshipped Lord.

Prayer preserves values and levels people. The rich and the poor, the leader and the subordinate, stand in one row, each sitting according to the order of his arrival. This produces a servitude-based equality in society; in prayer there is a sphere in which society becomes equal.

If prayer is the foundation of values, then zakah is the sustenance of the table for those who have no capacity to earn and work. Thus we have laws for life: for the continuity of the caliphate on earth, prayer sustains values and zakah sustains material provision.

Then He, glorified be He, says: ﴿And obey the Messenger, that you may receive mercy﴾ (al-Nur). Here, in connection with prayer and zakah, the Messenger was singled out for obedience, because he is the one who explains and details what Allah, glorified be He, stated in summary regarding the obligation of prayer and zakah, the details of each of which are found in the pure Sunnah. Thus He said: ﴿And obey the Messenger...﴾ (al-Nur).

(1) On the authority of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: "Take on of deeds what you are able to do, for Allah does not tire until you tire." Related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (1970), and likewise Muslim in his Sahih (782), Book of the Prayer of Travellers.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 24, verse 57:

Then the Truthful, glorified is He, says:

﴿Do not think that those who disbelieve will escape [Allah] in the earth, and their refuge is the Fire; and worst indeed is the destination.﴾

The context returns to speaking of the disbelievers: ﴿Do not think that those who disbelieve will escape [Allah] in the earth...﴾ (An-Nur). That is, do not suppose (لا تظنن). The word mu'jiz (معجز, "one who renders powerless") is that which establishes the incapacity of the opponent. We say: "We did a mu'jiz (معجزا) thing for so-and-so," meaning: he is unable to produce its like.

So beware lest you think that the disbelievers, however high their ranks and however far their tyranny spreads, will escape the punishment of Allah. They will never establish before Him, glorified is He, that they have rendered Him powerless, nor will they cause Him to be incapable. Rather, He, glorified is He, gives them respite and gives them time until, when He seizes them, He seizes them with the seizing of the Mighty, the Omnipotent. He, glorified is He, will surely overtake them.

It also came on the tongue of the jinn: ﴿And we thought that we would never cause Allah to be powerless in the earth, nor would we escape Him by flight.﴾ (Al-Jinn, 72:12)

We note in His saying, ﴿and their refuge is the Fire...﴾ (An-Nur), that this clause is conjoined to the preceding one, which is negated: ﴿Do not think...﴾ (An-Nur). Does this mean that its meaning is: "and do not think that their refuge is the Fire"? They said: No. Rather the meaning is: "and do not think that those who disbelieve will be powerless in the earth, because their refuge is the Fire."

﴿And worst indeed is the destination﴾ (An-Nur), that is: the return and the place of return.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 24, verse 58:

Then the context moves to a behaviour that touches society from within, and the family in its most private aspects, after it had mentioned at the beginning of the surah the rulings concerning external society. So He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess and those who have not yet reached puberty among you ask your permission at three times: before the prayer of dawn, and when you put off your clothing at midday, and after the prayer of night. Three times of nakedness (ʿawrah) for you. There is no sin upon you or upon them beyond these, as they go about attending to you, some of you to others. Thus does Allah make clear to you the verses, and Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾ 58

This verse teaches us the etiquette of seeking permission within the family made up of parents and children, and then the dependants such as servants and others. Allah, blessed and exalted, wishes to raise this family in the best possible manner, and here He addresses specifically those who have believed. That is, it means: O you who have believed in Me as Lord, Wise, Legislator for you, keen on your welfare, listen to this etiquette:

﴿Let those whom your right hands possess and those who have not yet reached puberty among you ask your permission three times...﴾ 58 (al-Nur).

It is well known that a speaker's demand upon an addressee comes in two forms: the imperative verb and the present-tense verb preceded by the imperative lām. So His saying ﴿liyastadhinkum﴾ (al-Nur): means: have these people be taught to ask your permission. Like ﴿walyastaʿfif alladhina la yajidun nikahan﴾ 33 (al-Nur): meaning: let them keep themselves chaste (istaʿfifu), because the lām here is the lām of command; and like ﴿liyunfiq dhu saʿatin min saʿatihi﴾ 7 (al-Talaq).

This etiquette is an obligation from Allah which every believer is charged with within the family, even though the command here is addressed to someone other than the one commanded. The ones commanded to seek permission are those whom the right hands possess and the young children. So Allah commanded the adults to teach the children, as the noble hadith has it: "Order your children to pray at seven, and strike them for it at ten" (1).

This obligation is not laid on the children; it is laid on the adults, because children have not yet reached the level of responsibility before their Lord; they have reached the level of responsibility only before you. Therefore it is you who command and you who follow up and hold to account (2).

The commanding of the child to pray or to seek permission is to train him in discipline and habit in a matter that may be hard for him when he is grown; if you accustom him to it now, it will be easy for him at the age of responsibility, and the habit will turn into an act of worship that he walks upon.

Allah has prescribed for us the etiquette of seeking permission because a person has an outward side that everyone sees, and he displays more of it to the intimate members of his household in matters he does not show to others. So: the intimacy of the family and those closest to you is wider, and there are social controls for the public society and social controls for the private society, which is the family. A person's freedom within his family is wider than his freedom in public society; if he is in his own private room, his freedom is wider than his freedom with the family.

So there must be controls that protect these privacies and regulate the relations of individuals within a single family, just as controls regulating relations of individuals outside the family have already preceded. As for the meaning of ﴿those whom your right hands possess﴾ (al-Nur): they are the slaves who serve some people, not the hired worker, because the hired worker is free and can leave you at any time; but the slave is not so, for he is owned in person and has no freedom. Ownership is dominant in these, and the master has control and authority, so he cannot escape from him.

﴿And those among you who have not yet reached puberty﴾ (al-Nur): they are the young children who have not reached the level of responsibility and who attend to needs; you see them in the house entering and leaving without controls, so shall we leave them thus to look upon our privacies?

The servants in the house have a nature that requires that they enter upon us and leave, and likewise the children, except at three times when they are not permitted to enter without seeking permission: ﴿before the prayer of dawn﴾ (al-Nur): because it is a time connected with sleep, and a person in sleep is free in movement and dress; ﴿and when you put off your clothing at midday﴾ (al-Nur): and this is the time of the afternoon rest (qaylulah), a time of repose in which a person lightens himself of his clothes; ﴿and after the prayer of night﴾ (al-Nur): and after the night prayer is sleep. These are three times, and no one should enter upon you in them except with your permission.

Consider this protection which your Lord, mighty and majestic, provides for you, so that your freedom in your personal affairs and private matters is not restricted, as if these times were yours, O believer, in which you take your ease and enjoy your privacy; and seeking permission gives you the opportunity to prepare to meet the one seeking entry.

As for the rest of the times, everyone seeks permission to enter upon you, even the wife.

The occasion of revelation of this verse is that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wanted Sayyidna ʿUmar about a certain matter, so he sent to him a boy (3) from the Ansar. When the boy went, he pushed the door and called out: "O ʿUmar!" while he was sleeping in a state in which no one should be seen by anyone. ʿUmar woke up and noticed that the boy had seen him in this state. When he went to the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "O Messenger of Allah, we want our sons, our women, our clients and our servants to seek permission to enter upon us, for such-and-such has happened from the boy," and so this verse was revealed (4).

Allah calls these three times ʿawrah: ﴿Three times of nakedness (ʿawrah) for you﴾ 58 (al-Nur). ʿAwrah is that which a person dislikes that anyone should see, or see him in; because it is a kind of defect and privacy, and Allah does not want anyone to see you in something you dislike.

For this reason they say of one with a defect in his eye, for example: aʿwar (one-eyed/defective). And the Arabs say of an ugly word: ʿawraʾ (5), as the poet said: "An ugly word came from a brother, so I returned it with a sound-eyed reply, seeking excuse (lit. two sound eyes)" (6). That is: an ugly word, which I did not answer with its like, but with soundness not of one eye, rather with the soundness of both eyes.

Then He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿There is no sin upon you or upon them beyond these﴾ (al-Nur): that is, after these times there is no sin or blame upon you, nor upon the slaves or the children, if they enter upon you; for outside these times a person sits prepared to carry on his ordinary life, and he has no objection to receiving servants or young children without seeking permission, because the nature of living in houses cannot do without their entering and leaving constantly.

For this reason He, Exalted, said after it: ﴿as they go about attending to you, some of you to others﴾ (al-Nur): that is, their movement in the house is continuous, entering and leaving; so how could we restrict it outside these times?

﴿Thus does Allah make clear to you the verses﴾ (al-Nur): that is, a clear explanation, so that no contradictions arise in society afterwards. ﴿And Allah is Knowing﴾ (al-Nur): of everything that suits the vicegerency on earth. ﴿Wise﴾ (al-Nur): in His legislation and commands, He sets no ruling except with wisdom.

Then the Almighty says:

﴿And when the children among you reach puberty, let them ask permission as those before them asked permission. Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ (24:59)

The child, while he was a child who had not reached puberty, used to enter without seeking permission at times other than these. But if he reaches puberty, it becomes obligatory upon him to seek permission. We do not say that he should only become accustomed to seeking permission at these times; no, rather he must seek permission at all times, for he has grown up and matured, and this status has ended for him.

Puberty (bulugh al-hulm) is when a person matures to the point of becoming fit to beget offspring like himself. This is the sign that his creation has been completed, and this can only come about through the completion of the sexual instinct, which is the cause of procreation and reproduction. We may illustrate this with fruit, which is not sweet except after it ripens. If you leave it after ripening, it falls of its own accord. This is one of the signs of Allah for the preservation of the species: if we ate the fruit before it ripened, its seed would not sprout and its kind would become extinct. So it is part of Allah's wisdom in creation that fruit is not sweet until it has ripened.

Likewise, when the boy reaches puberty he becomes fit for procreation, and we say to him: the concession that the Law granted you has ended, and you must seek permission at all times.

For this reason the Exalted says in another place: ﴿or the children who have not yet come to know the private aspects of women…﴾ (24:31).

He used the singular "al-tifl" (the child), because children at this age have not yet developed the instinct and do not have these inclinations or desires, so they are as one. But after puberty, when the instinctive inclinations have formed, He said ﴿al-atfal﴾ (the children), because each of them, after puberty, has his own inclinations, personality and deviations.

His saying ﴿as those before them asked permission﴾ means: the adults who seek permission at all times. ﴿Thus﴾ means: just as We explained the first permission. ﴿Allah makes clear to you His verses﴾ — because He ﴿is All-Knowing﴾ of what sets you right, ﴿All-Wise﴾: He does not legislate for you except with wisdom.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 24, verse 60:

Then He, glorified is He, says:

﴿And as for women past child-bearing who have no hope of marriage, there is no blame upon them if they put aside their outer garments without displaying adornment. But to refrain is better for them. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾

We know that the Wise Lawgiver established for the Muslim woman principles by which she is to conduct herself in her dress, her behaviour and her manner of walking, as protection for her and as a safeguard for society against temptation, and so that those with diseased hearts do not covet her. He therefore made for her a veil that covers her and conceals her adornment, not one that is transparent or descriptive, and He said: ﴿They should draw their outer garments (jalabib) over themselves...﴾ [33:59].

However, women who are past child-bearing (al-qawa'id) and the elderly among them have a different ruling.

Al-qawa'id is the plural of qa'id, not qa'ida. Qa'ida indicates sitting, whereas the qa'id, whether male or female, is one who has withdrawn from the cycle of life and no longer has the function of bearing children. Such women no longer have any desire (irba) or any object of desire (matma'), so there is no objection to their lightening somewhat the clothing that was imposed on them when temptation exists, and she may, for example, set aside her headscarf (tarha).

But this matter is subject to degrees and is relative: some women's menstruation ceases and old age overtakes them, yet beauty and allure may still remain in them. Therefore our Lord, blessed and exalted is He, set down for us a precautionary ruling: ﴿there is no blame upon them if they put aside their outer garments without displaying adornment...﴾ [24:60]. It is not permissible for a woman to put off her clothing relying on this concession and then display her adornment and make herself visible. We fear that if we teach women this ruling they will act upon it without restraint, and we would then be saying of them that they are qawa'id!

It is remarkable that when a woman reaches this age you find her modest in her clothing, modest in her appearance, modest in her conduct, so she grows in beauty, splendour and attractiveness. This is unlike the one who does not respect her age, who puts on cosmetics and colours on her face and so appears as a disfigured caricature.

The meaning of ﴿yasta'finna...﴾ [24:60] is: they keep their clothing on and do not remove any of it, for this is more conducive to chastity.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 24, verse 61:

﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor is there blame upon the lame, nor is there blame upon the sick, nor upon yourselves, that you eat from your houses, or the houses of your fathers, or the houses of your mothers, or the houses of your brothers, or the houses of your sisters, or the houses of your paternal uncles, or the houses of your paternal aunts, or the houses of your maternal uncles, or the houses of your maternal aunts, or from that whose keys you possess, or from the house of your friend. There is no blame upon you for eating together or separately. So when you enter houses, greet one another with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good. Thus Allah makes the signs clear to you, that you may understand.﴾

The Almighty's words: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor is there blame upon the lame, nor is there blame upon the sick...﴾ Al-haraj (blame, constriction) means narrowness, as in His saying: ﴿And whoever Allah wills to leave astray, He makes his breast narrow and constricted, as if he were climbing into the sky...﴾ [al-An'am 6:125].

Or haraj may mean sin, so the blame lifted from these people is constriction or sin connected with the ruling that follows concerning eating, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿nor upon yourselves...﴾ [al-Nur 24:61].

The blind man feels constrained about eating with people, because he cannot see his food, and his hand may reach for the best food and eat it while leaving the lesser. The lame man needs a special ease in his sitting, and may burden others with that. The sick person may be disliked by people for his condition. So Allah the Exalted lifted this constraint from His servants, and said: ﴿There is no blame upon you for eating together or separately...﴾ [al-Nur 24:61].

Thus it is correct to eat together, because the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, wants to make completeness lie in the essences and not in the accidents. Also, if you see a young man afflicted (mu'awwaf)(1), meaning he has a calamity, and then you treat him with a special treatment, you may wound his feelings, even if what he has is a created matter from Allah that he cannot reject. Some people refuse that Allah should create them in a form they do not accept.

Therefore, in the countryside we used to hear them say: "Whoever gives blindness its due is sighted." Why? Because he accepts this trial and deals with people on that basis, so he asks them for help. Hence you see all the people racing to help him and take him by the hand. If he has lost one eye, Allah has compensated him with a thousand eyes. As for the one who refuses and rejects acknowledging his incapacity, and wears dark glasses to hide his defect, he walks with difficulty, stumbling, and no one helps him.

It is as if the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, wants the people of these afflictions to be in harmony with society: they take no stance against it, and society takes no stance against them(2). Therefore He joins: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor is there blame upon the lame, nor is there blame upon the sick...﴾ [al-Nur 24:61], then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿nor upon yourselves...﴾ [al-Nur 24:61], meaning: they are exactly like you, so there is no blame between you in anything.

﴿That you eat from your houses...﴾ [al-Nur 24:61], etc.

Among the Ansar there was a man of qazzaza(3): when he sat in a house he would not eat from it unless the owner of the house permitted him. A man among them might travel and leave his servant in the house without permitting him to eat from the food of the house, and then return and find the food as it was, or find it spoiled without the servant having eaten anything from it. So the Truth, glorified is He, wished to lift this constraint from people, and said: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick, nor upon yourselves that you eat from your houses...﴾ [al-Nur 24:61], to the end of these coordinated items.

One might say: what blame is there in a person eating from his own house? Would it ever occur to anyone that he would find blame in eating from his own house?

They said: If you try to enumerate these relatives mentioned in the verse, the answer will become clear to you. The verse mentions your fathers, your mothers, your brothers, your sisters, your paternal uncles, your paternal aunts, your maternal uncles and your maternal aunts, but it mentions nothing about the children, although they are at the head of this order. Why?

They said: Because the houses of the children are the houses of the fathers, and when you eat from your son's house it is as if you are eating from your own house, on the basis that the son and what his hands possess belong to his father. So you may substitute for ﴿your houses...﴾ [al-Nur 24:61]: the houses of your children. That is because the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, did not want to give the children houses separate from the fathers, since they are one thing.

So there is no blame upon you in eating from the house of your son, your father, your mother, your brother, your sister, your paternal uncle, your paternal aunt, your maternal uncle or your maternal aunt, ﴿or from that whose keys you possess...﴾ [al-Nur 24:61]: meaning the owner of the house gives you the key to his house(4), and in this is permission for you to dispose of it and eat from its food if you wish.

﴿Or your friend...﴾ [al-Nur 24:61]: You will notice that this is the only one that came in the singular form in this verse. Before it: your houses, your fathers, your mothers... etc., but for the friend He said ﴿or your friend...﴾ [al-Nur 24:61], and did not say "your friends."

That is because the word friend (sadiq), like the word enemy (adu), is used for the group in the singular, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For they are enemies to me...﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:77].

Because even if they are a group, they must be of one heart, otherwise they would not be friends. Likewise in the case of enmity we say "enemy," though they are plural, because enemies are united by hatred, so they are as one.

Then the Almighty says: ﴿There is no blame upon you for eating together or separately...﴾ [al-Nur 24:61]. ﴿Together...﴾ [al-Nur 24:61]: side by side, some of you with others. ﴿Or separately...﴾ [al-Nur 24:61]: scattered, each alone.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when you enter houses, greet one another(5) with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good...﴾ [al-Nur 24:61]: "greet one another," because when you greet another it is as if you greet yourself, since the other will also greet you. That is because Islam wants to make the community of faith a cohesive unity. So when you say to another, "Peace be upon you," he will reply, "And upon you be peace." It is as if you have greeted yourself.

Or the meaning is: if you enter houses in which there is no one, then greet yourselves. When they enter the mosque they say: "Peace be upon the Messenger of Allah, and upon us from our Lord." They said: The angels hear and return it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿A greeting from Allah, blessed and good...﴾ [al-Nur 24:61]. In another verse He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And when you are greeted with a greeting, greet with better than it, or return it...﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:86].

The greeting, beyond being from Allah, He described as ﴿blessed...﴾ [al-Nur 24:61]. A blessed thing is that which gives more than what is expected from it. ﴿Thus...﴾ [al-Nur 24:61]: that is, just as He made clear to you the previous rulings, He makes clear to you ﴿the signs, that you may understand﴾ [al-Nur 24:61].

That is: the Lord who has imposed these rulings upon you loves good for you, and He is independent of these. He only commands you with things whose benefit returns to you. If you obey Him in what He has commanded you, you benefit from His commands in this world, and then His reward and recompense await you in the Hereafter.

1 Mu'awwaf: afflicted by a calamity. Al-afah is the defect. Affa al-bilad: the land became afflicted. (Lisan al-Arab, root: a-w-f).
2 Ibn 'Abbas said: When Allah the Blessed and Exalted revealed ﴿And do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood...﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:188], the Muslims refrained from eating with the sick, the disabled and the lame, saying: food is the best of wealth, and Allah has forbidden consuming wealth in falsehood, and the blind man cannot see the good food, and the sick man does not fully enjoy the food. So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor is there blame upon the lame...﴾ [al-Nur 24:61]. (Cited by al-Wahidi in Asbab al-Nuzul, p. 189).
3 Al-qazzaza: shame. Qazzat nafsi 'an al-shay': I rejected it and found it repugnant. Taqazzaza al-rajul min al-shay': the man did not eat or drink it by his own will. (Lisan al-Arab, root: q-z-z).
4 On the authority of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, he used to say regarding this verse: it was revealed concerning people who, when they went out with the Prophet (ﷺ), would place the keys of their houses with the blind, the lame, the sick and with their relatives, and would tell them to eat from what is in their houses if they needed it, but they themselves would be wary of eating from them, saying: we fear their hearts would not be content with that. So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. (Cited by al-Wahidi in Asbab al-Nuzul, p. 190).
5 Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (6/4857): "The more correct view is that this is general for entering any house. If there is a Muslim resident, he says: 'Peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah and His blessings.' If there is no resident, he says: 'Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah.' And if there is in the house someone who is not a Muslim, he says: 'Peace be upon those who follow the guidance,' or 'Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah.'"

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿The believers are only those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger, and when they are with him on a matter of common concern (1), they do not leave until they have asked his permission. Indeed, those who ask your permission are the ones who believe in Allah and His Messenger. So when they ask your permission for some of their affairs, give permission to whom you will among them and ask forgiveness for them from Allah. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ 62

The believer: he who has believed in God and believed in the Messenger who conveys from God. Since you have believed in the Messenger who conveys from God, your movement must necessarily be subject to his commands, and your self must belong to him. When the Messenger sees a matter of common concern that gathers the Muslims, whether in a sermon, an event, or a war, and then calls you to consultation (shura) so that each of you may offer his opinion and experience, and widens the scope of consultation in the community so that the judgment comes out sound, correct, and in accordance with the general interest.

So the true believer, when he is called to such a common matter, does not rise from his assembly until he has asked permission of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is not obligatory that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) grant him permission, because the common matter of the Muslims may be more important than the matter that preoccupies you and that you wish to rise for, leaving the assembly of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who ask your permission are the ones who believe in Allah and His Messenger...﴾ 62 (al-Nur): here, asking permission is one of the signs of faith. One does not slip away (yansallu) from the gathering stealthily, unnoticed by anyone. He must ask the Messenger of Allah's permission, so that no benefit is lost to the believers, and perhaps he has an opinion that would benefit them.

The Messenger consults his companions only to be enlightened by their opinions and experiences. So when he calls them to a common matter, this matter must be understood in the context of the Messenger's station in conveying from God to the community. If a man calls a few men for consultation, they consult about a personal matter that concerns its owner. But when the Messenger of Allah calls them, he does not call for a single private concern, but for the concern of a community that God willed to be the best community brought forth for mankind. He too will benefit from this call, and perhaps his benefit from responding to the general call that embraces all people is greater than his benefit from his private call. So the one who is called must weigh this difference.

Despite this difference, God did not deprive those people who have preoccupations of asking permission from the Messenger and leaving; therefore He legislated asking permission for them. But they must keep this difference in mind, and remember that they left for some of their affairs, while the Messenger stands in matters of the affairs of this world entirely until the Hour comes.

So if he participates in this gathering, he will benefit as an individual, and his community will benefit: those of them present and those who come after until the Hour comes. If he prefers his personal matter over these affairs, he has done wrong and acted in a way unbecoming of a believer. Therefore the Messenger of Allah was commanded to give permission to whom he wills, and then ask forgiveness for him from Allah.

He, glorified is He, says: ﴿So when they ask your permission for some of their affairs, give permission to whom you will among them...﴾ 62 (al-Nur): the matter is left to the Messenger of Allah, who estimates it according to the general interest of the Muslims, so he may grant permission or withhold it.

So: asking the permission of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is necessary, and he grants permission to whom he wills among them, those whom he sees that the rest can compensate for him and his opinion. If a man of opinion from whom the Muslims would benefit asks permission, he does not grant it to him.

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿and ask forgiveness for them from Allah...﴾ 62 (al-Nur). As if the matter of asking permission and rising from the assembly of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is something God does not desire.

Even if you ask permission for a matter that concerns you, and even if the Messenger of Allah grants you permission, the better course is not to ask permission, because when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) calls to a common matter that concerns the body of the Muslims, no one should be preoccupied from what he was called to, nor should he give precedence to anything else over the interest of the Muslims and the assembly of the Messenger of Allah. In a common matter, everyone should gather their talents and thoughts on the subject. When you ask permission for a matter that concerns you, you are preoccupied away from the community and distracted from them.

When you become preoccupied with your private matter instead of the general matter of the Muslims, this is a matter that requires you to seek forgiveness from the Messenger of Allah, so the Messenger grants you permission, and then asks Allah's forgiveness for you.

(1) It has been differed concerning what the common matter is. It was said: what is meant by it is what the Imam needs to gather people for in order to proclaim an interest, such as establishing a sunnah in religion, or to frighten an enemy by their gathering, and for wars. Makhul and al-Zuhri said: Friday prayer is among the common matters. (Tafsir al-Qurtubi 6/4858).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 24, verse 63:

Then the Truthful, Glorified One says:

﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among yourselves like the calling of some of you to others. Allah already knows those of you who slip away, clinging to one another. So let those who oppose his command beware lest a trial befall them or a painful punishment strike them.﴾

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among yourselves like the calling of some of you to others...﴾ (al-Nur): You call one another about a particular matter, but the Messenger calls you to a general matter that concerns the movement of the lives of all people until the Hour arises.

Or: the word "calling" (du'a') here means "summoning" (nida'), meaning: the Messenger summons you, or you summon him. For the summoning of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has manners that must be observed. He is not like one of you whom you address as "O Muhammad." The Qur'an has rebuked a group who did not observe the manners of addressing the Messenger of Allah, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the chambers, most of them do not reason.﴾ (al-Hujurat, 4).

They erred when they said, "O Muhammad." Even if they had said, "O Messenger," they would still have erred, because it is not proper for them to hasten the Messenger of Allah; they must leave him at ease. If he finds leisure to meet them, he comes out to them. Thus they erred in two respects.

It is also not fitting that we address him (ﷺ) by his name, "O Muhammad," because what unites the Messenger with his community is not that he is Muhammad; rather, what unites them is that he is the Messenger of Allah, so we must address him by this description. And why not? His Lord, Mighty and Majestic, who created him and chose him, has distinguished him from the rest of his brother messengers and from the messengers of firm resolve. He addressed them by their names:

﴿O Adam, dwell you and your wife in the Garden...﴾ (al-Baqara, 35).

And He said: ﴿O Noah, descend with peace from Us...﴾ (Hud, 48).

And He said: ﴿O Abraham, you have indeed fulfilled the vision...﴾ (al-Saffat, 104-105).

And He said: ﴿O Moses, indeed I am Allah...﴾ (al-Qasas, 30).

And He said: ﴿O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people...﴾ (al-Ma'ida, 116).

And He said: ﴿O David, indeed We have made you a successor in the earth...﴾ (Sad, 26).

But the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was never addressed by his name at all; rather, he was addressed with "O you who..." — "O Messenger," "O Prophet." If the Truthful, Blessed and Exalted, did not make His calling to the Messenger like His calling to his other messengers, shall we call him by his name? We should say: "O Messenger," "O Prophet," "O Messenger of Allah," "O Prophet of Allah." This is the fitting and honoring description.

Just as we distinguish the calling of the Messenger of Allah when we summon him, so too when he summons us we must respect this summons, knowing that this summons is for a general good whose benefit returns to everyone.

Then the Truthful, Glorified One says: ﴿Allah already knows those of you who slip away, clinging to one another. So let those who oppose his command beware lest a trial befall them or a painful punishment strike them.﴾ (al-Nur, 63).

There is no doubt that those who seek the Messenger of Allah's permission have faith; they observe the gathering of the Messenger and do not rise except with his permission. But there are others who rise without asking permission: ﴿slip away...﴾ (al-Nur, 63). Tasallul (slipping away) is leaving gradually and secretly, such as shifting from one place to another until one exits, or making you think he wants to speak with another person so that he rises and slips quietly out of the gathering. This is the meaning of ﴿slip away from you, clinging...﴾ (al-Nur, 63): he clings to another in order to leave because of him.

Allah warns these people: ﴿So let those who oppose his command beware...﴾ (al-Nur, 63). Tahdhir (warning) is a notice of the evil consequence that follows from withdrawing from the Messenger's gathering, as if He is saying to them: compare your withdrawal from the Messenger's gathering with the punishment awaiting you for it.

He said: ﴿those who oppose his command...﴾ (al-Nur, 63): they do not oppose his command, so He made in opposition the meaning of turning away, not mere opposition. So the meaning is: they turn away from it.

And "command" (amr) may mean an imperative or prohibitive form, or the matter we are concerned with. Here it is not a request; this meaning is what is intended here: that is, the matter we are examining and discussing. So consider what the Messenger of Allah said, and do not oppose or contradict him, for even though he is a human being like you, he is one to whom revelation is given.

Therefore the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) defined his position as a human being and as a messenger. He said: "I am asked by my Lord, meaning from the Highest Truth, and I say: I am not like any of you; and when I am asked of something, I say: I am only a human being like you."

Accordingly, the Companions understood this matter and observed its etiquette with the Messenger of Allah, and they would ask him about a matter: is it from Allah, has revelation been sent down concerning it, or is it opinion and counsel? If the matter had revelation from Allah, there is no speech for anyone against the word of Allah; and if nothing had been revealed from Allah concerning it, each of them would give his opinion and counsel.

This actually happened at the Battle of Badr, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stopped at a position that some of the Companions thought was not the best. They asked the Messenger of Allah: "Is this a position Allah has caused you to alight at, or is it opinion and counsel?" He said: "Rather, it is opinion and counsel." So they informed him that it was not suitable, and that the suitable place was such and such.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿lest a trial befall them...﴾ (al-Nur, 63): that is, in this world; ﴿or a painful punishment strike them﴾ (al-Nur, 63): that is, in the Hereafter. Even if they escape the trial of this world, they will not escape the punishment of the Hereafter.

(1) Al-Habbab ibn al-Mundhir ibn al-Jamuh said: "O Messenger of Allah, do you regard this position as one Allah has caused you to alight at, which we may not advance beyond or fall behind, or is it opinion, war and stratagem?" He said: "Rather, it is opinion, war and stratagem." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is not a suitable position; rise with the people until we come to the nearest water of the enemy and occupy it," and the hadith continues. It is cited by Ibn Hisham in al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (2/620), quoting Ibn Ishaq.

Then He concluded the surah with His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Surely to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. He knows your state, and on the Day they are returned to Him He will inform them of what they did. And God is All-Knowing of everything.﴾ (24:64)

Alā (ألا): an interjection of alerting (tanbīh) to something important that follows. Alerting comes because speech is a kind of messenger between the speaker and the addressee. The speaker usually prepares his speech and is familiar with what he will say, but the addressee may not be free of thought, so the utterance surprises him, perhaps distracts him, and some of it is lost to him.

The Truth, blessed and exalted, wants that not a single letter of His speech be lost to you, so He alerts you with a word that in itself has, in reality, no meaning, yet it wakes you and dispels whatever astonishment or heedlessness you have, so that you comprehend what is said to you. This is an Arabic usage that the Arabs knew and spoke before the Qur'an was revealed.

The pre-Islamic poet says, addressing the woman who hands him the cup:

Alā, hubbī bi-ṣaḥnki fa-aṣbiḥīnā
wa-lā tubqī khumūra l-Andarīnā¹

He wants to alert her to the useful speech that comes after.

After the alerting alā, He, glorified, says: ﴿Surely to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth…﴾ The heavens and the earth are containers, within which is everything in the upper and lower cosmos. So "what is in the heavens and in the earth" means: what is contained within them. Then what about the container itself? They said: it too belongs to God, as occurs in another verse: ﴿To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth…﴾ (24:42). Thus the container and the contained are both His possession, glorified is He.

The container is usually less valuable than what it contains: what is inside a treasury, for example, is more precious than it, and what is inside a bag is more precious than it. Likewise, the greatness of the heavens and the earth lies in the creatures within them. Therefore beware of making the noble Qur'an a container for something important to you, keeping it within the Qur'an: nothing is more precious or valuable than the Book of God, so it is not fitting to make it a holder for your money or your important papers, because what is kept is usually more valuable than the thing in which it is kept.

In the verse ﴿Surely to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth…﴾ (24:64) there is a restrictive construction (qaṣr) through the fronting of the prepositional phrase: everything in the heavens and everything in the earth belongs to God alone, with no partner. Despite the multitude of those who falsely claim divinity and Pharaohship, none of them has claimed to possess any part of it.

Even Nimrod, who disputed with our father Abraham, peace be upon him, and said, "I give life and cause death," when Abraham said to him: ﴿Indeed God brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west…﴾ (2:258), was unable to do anything, was confounded, and the matter ended.

His dominion, exalted is He, is not confined to creation. He did not create things and then leave them to perform their functions alone; rather He created them while possessing al-qayyūmiyya (sustaining authority) over what He created, and disposing of everything. So do not suppose that the cosmos around you serves you mechanically; it is subject to the will of God and His disposal, glorified is He.

The water that flows to you from rain and rivers may be withheld from you, so your land suffers drought, or it may exceed its limit, becoming torrents that drown and destroy. So the matter is not a mere routine of creation, and creatures are not machines; rather, to God belong the dominion, the sustaining authority, and the disposal of all that He created.

Then He, glorified, says: ﴿He knows your state…﴾ (24:64). To understand this verse we must know that the relation of the Truth, blessed and exalted, to events is not like our relation. We know from grammar that verbs are past (māḍī), which is what has already occurred before you speak it, such as "Muḥammad came"; and present (muḍāriʿ), which is either for the present, such as "Muḥammad eats," or for the future, such as "Muḥammad will eat."

As for God, exalted is He, all events are equal: all are past and occurring. We have discussed this matter in His saying: ﴿The command of God has come, so do not seek to hasten it…﴾ (16:1).

It is known that seeking to hasten is for a matter that has not yet come, and the Resurrection has not yet come, yet it is expressed in the past tense (atā, "has come"), because nothing hinders Him or takes Him out of His will, so it is as though it has already come. Thus ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾ (16:1) is not logical with your speech but is logical with the speech of God.

Likewise in His saying: ﴿He knows your state…﴾ (24:64): qad (قد) is for emphasis (taḥqīq), and yaʿlamu (يعلم) with respect to God means knowledge, but with respect to you it means "He knows." So there is a part from you and a part from the Truth, glorified is He: for the emphasis He used qad, and for the future He used yaʿlamu.

Then He, glorified, says: ﴿and on the Day they are returned to Him He will inform them of what they did, and God is All-Knowing of everything﴾ (24:64). In another verse: ﴿Not an atom's weight in the earth or in the heaven escapes your Lord, nor anything smaller than that or greater, but it is in a clear Book﴾ (10:61).

Beware of understanding that God's seeing and regard of the various parts in different places is a partial vision, turning to one thing and not perceiving another. Rather it is a comprehensive vision, as though each thing had a vision of its own. This is clear in His saying: ﴿Is He who is standing over every soul in what it has earned…?﴾ (13:33).

He, glorified, is not occupied by one hearing from another, nor one sight from another; His sight is all-encompassing and His observation is precise. Therefore His recompense comes as a true match to the precision of His observation. So beware of neglecting this truth: your Lord is standing over you, watching you; nothing of you is hidden from Him.

So, O you who slip away furtively, beware! Nothing is more important than sitting in the assembly of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace. The Messenger of God himself was eager to see his companions in his assembly continually, and God, may He be exalted, enjoined this upon him, saying: ﴿And let not your eyes pass beyond them…﴾ (18:28).

Some of his companions prayed behind him. When he finished the salam, the man would leave hastily, and the Prophet, peace be upon him, would see him at the beginning of the prayer but not see him at its end. So on one occasion he stopped him and said: "Is it indifference toward us?" As though it grieved the Messenger of God that one of his companions should not be present in his presence, or should shun his assembly, and so be deprived of the goods and the illuminations that descend upon the assembly of the Messenger of God, and be deprived of the radiance of his insight and his sight directed toward him.

Therefore the man was embarrassed, and began to explain to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, what drove him to hurry away after every prayer, and that this on his part was not indifference toward the presence of the Messenger of God or his assembly. He said: "O Messenger of God, I have a wife at home who is waiting for this cloak of mine so she can pray in it."

That is: he had only one garment in his house. The Prophet, peace be upon him, prayed good for him. When he returned to his wife she asked him about the reason for his absence, so he related to her what had passed with the Messenger of God, that he had stopped him and recounted to her what had passed between them. She said to her husband: "Are you complaining of your Lord to Muḥammad?"

When they later asked her, she said: "He was absent from me for about a hundred tasbīḥas." Look at the time-keeping by which she regulated her hour.
